title: Column buckling: Euler, the effective length, and why the code says less
summary: Run a linear buckling Step on a pinned–pinned S355 column, check the eigenvalue against π²EI/(KL)², and see why the EN 1993-1-1 buckling curve puts the design resistance at about 60 % of it.

steps.title: Start a Model
steps.explain: A column is the one structural member whose strength has almost nothing to do with its stress. This tutorial computes the load at which a straight column stops wanting to stay straight, and then says plainly why that number is not the load you may design to.

steps.title: Units
steps.explain: Millimetres, kilonewtons, megapascals. A buckling factor is dimensionless and comes back the same in any unit system.

steps.title: Half a column
steps.explain: The column is 200 × 200 mm and 5 m between pins, but the Body is only 2.5 m tall. The first buckling mode is a half sine wave, symmetric about mid-height, so modelling the lower half with a symmetry plane at the top is exact for it and halves the cost. Keep the real length in mind: every formula below uses L = 5 m, not the 2.5 m on screen.

steps.title: S355
steps.explain: Only `E` enters the eigenvalue — buckling is a stiffness problem, and the yield strength never appears in Euler's formula. It appears at the very end, in the code check, and that is exactly the point of this tutorial.

steps.title: Mesh it, quadratic
steps.explain: Twenty hex20 elements up the half-height and three across each section dimension. A buckling mode is a bending shape, so the elements have to bend well: `order: 2` matters far more here than element count. Refining to 4 × 4 × 40 moves the answer by 0.14 %, so this mesh is converged enough to compare with a closed form.

steps.title: Pin the foot
steps.explain: `ux` and `uy` on the bottom face, and deliberately not `uz`. That holds the base against sliding sideways while leaving it free to rotate — which is what a pin is. Holding `uz` on the whole face as well would keep the end section horizontal, and that is a fixed base: the same column would then come out roughly twice as strong.

steps.title: Symmetry at mid-height
steps.explain: `uz = 0` on the top face of the half model. At mid-height of a half-sine mode the section neither rises nor rotates, so this is the mode's own symmetry condition, not a restraint that changes it — and it is what carries the applied load, so the Result's balance check closes on zero. It does hide the antisymmetric modes, the full-sine shape at four times the load among them; ask for those and you would model the whole column.

steps.title: A reference load of 1 MPa
steps.explain: A buckling Step does not need the real load: it reports the factor by which whatever you apply must be multiplied. Applying exactly 1 MPa over 40 000 mm² makes the reference load 40 kN — and makes the eigenvalue read directly as the critical stress in MPa, which is convenient to compare with f_y.

steps.title: A buckling Step, two modes
steps.explain: `procedure: buckling` first solves the static state under the reference load, then the eigenproblem that uses its stresses. Two modes, because the section is square: bending about the two axes is equally easy, so the first two eigenvalues are a degenerate pair, the same load in two perpendicular planes. Two identical numbers is the answer, not a bug — and a warning that the real column has no preferred direction to fall in.

steps.title: Solve, and read the factor
steps.explain: Both factors come back at 272.81. Multiply by the 40 kN reference load: the column buckles at about 10 900 kN. The mode shape is the quarter sine of the modelled half — it has no magnitude, only a shape, which is why a buckling plot has no useful contour scale.

steps.title: Euler, K, slenderness — and the design value
steps.explain: What the eigenvalue is, what it is not, and how EN 1993-1-1 turns it into a resistance.
steps.theory:
**The eigenvalue.** A linear buckling Step solves $(K + \lambda K_g)\varphi = 0$, where $K_g$ is the geometric stiffness built from the stress state of the reference load. $\lambda$ is the factor on that load at which the column has a second equilibrium shape $\varphi$ beside the straight one. The reference pressure was $1\,\mathrm{MPa}$ on $200 \times 200 = 40\,000\,\mathrm{mm}^2$, so $P_{\mathrm{ref}} = 40\,\mathrm{kN}$ and

$$P_{cr} = \lambda P_{\mathrm{ref}} = 272.81 \times 40 = \mathbf{10\,912\,\mathrm{kN}}$$

Because the reference pressure was exactly 1 MPa, $\lambda$ is also the critical stress in megapascals: $\sigma_{cr} = 272.8\,\mathrm{MPa}$.

**Euler.** For a prismatic elastic column,

$$P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{(KL)^2}, \qquad I = \frac{b^4}{12} = 1.3333\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{mm}^4$$

With $K = 1$, $E = 210\,\mathrm{GPa}$ and $L = 5\,\mathrm{m}$ that is $11\,054\,\mathrm{kN}$. The solved value sits $1.3\,\%$ below it, and the gap is physics plus discretisation rather than error: Euler's formula assumes bending only, while a solid column also shears. Engesser's correction $P_{cr} = P_E/(1 + P_E/GA_s)$ with $A_s = \tfrac{5}{6}A$ gives $11\,009\,\mathrm{kN}$, $0.4\,\%$ down, and the rest is the mesh together with the end faces being held flat in $u_x$ and $u_y$ rather than resting on a frictionless knife edge. Refining to $4 \times 4 \times 40$ moves the answer to $273.18$, converging from below.

**The effective length $K$.** The same formula covers every classic end condition; only $K$ changes, and it is the *half-wavelength of the buckled shape* divided by $L$:

- pinned–pinned: $K = 1.0$ — the case solved above, $P_{cr} = 1.00\,P_E$.
- fixed–fixed: $K = 0.5$ — $4.00\,P_E$.
- fixed–pinned: $K = 0.699$ — $2.05\,P_E$.
- fixed–free (a cantilever column, or an unbraced storey): $K = 2.0$ — $0.25\,P_E$.

A fixed base is worth a factor of two to four, which is why the base detail of a column is worth arguing about. In practice nothing is ideal, and design guidance raises the theoretical $K$ (AISC, for instance, recommends 0.65, 0.80 and 1.2 for the three restrained cases) because a real connection rotates.

**Slenderness.** $i = \sqrt{I/A} = b/\sqrt{12} = 57.7\,\mathrm{mm}$, so $\lambda = L/i = 86.6$. With $\lambda_1 = 93.9\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon = \sqrt{235/f_y} = 0.814$ for S355, $\lambda_1 = 76.4$ and the relative slenderness is

$$\bar{\lambda} = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda_1} = 1.13 \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \bar{\lambda} = \sqrt{\frac{A f_y}{N_{cr}}} = \sqrt{\frac{14\,200}{10\,912}} = 1.14$$

**Why the design value is lower — and why the eigenvalue is not one.** This number is an upper bound on strength, not a load you may design to. It assumes a perfectly straight member, a load exactly on the centroid, no residual stress from rolling or welding, and material that stays elastic. A real column has an initial bow of roughly $L/1000$, so it bends from the first kilonewton; residual stresses yield the flange tips early and shrink the effective section; and once yielding starts the tangent stiffness drops below $E$. EN 1993-1-1 §6.3.1 packages all of that into a reduction factor:

$$N_{b,Rd} = \frac{\chi A f_y}{\gamma_{M1}}, \qquad \chi = \frac{1}{\Phi + \sqrt{\Phi^2 - \bar{\lambda}^2}} \le 1, \qquad \Phi = 0.5\left[1 + \alpha(\bar{\lambda} - 0.2) + \bar{\lambda}^2\right]$$

A solid section takes buckling curve c (EN 1993-1-1 Table 6.2), $\alpha = 0.49$. At $\bar{\lambda} = 1.14$ that gives $\Phi = 1.381$ and $\chi = 0.463$, so with $\gamma_{M1} = 1.0$

$$N_{b,Rd} = 0.463 \times 40\,000 \times 355 = \mathbf{6\,575\,\mathrm{kN}}$$

about **60 % of the eigenvalue**, and well under the squash load $A f_y = 14\,200\,\mathrm{kN}$ that a stub of the same section would carry. Use the eigenvalue to find out *how* the column wants to fail and at what order of magnitude, and to compare schemes; use the buckling curve to size it.
